content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed comprehensive antenatal care (ANC) guidelines aimed at improving the quality of routine healthcare provided to all women and adolescent girls during pregnancy. These guidelines were first published in 2016 with the overarching goal of ensuring a positive pregnancy experience for all pregnant individuals. This principle encourages countries to expand their healthcare agendas beyond mere survival, focusing instead on maximizing health outcomes, human rights, and the potential of their populations. ANC serves as a strategic platform for essential healthcare functions, including health promotion and disease prevention. Of the 49 recommendations in the 2016 WHO ANC guideline, 14 are specifically related to nutritional interventions during pregnancy. In April 2019, the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) prioritized two antenatal nutrition recommendations for updating based on new evidence. These were: (1) vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy and (2) multiple micronutrient supplementation during pregnancy. The evidence for these interventions was reviewed by an international Guideline Development Group (GDG) during an online meeting held on December 4–5, 2019. The recommendations were updated following WHO’s living guidelines approach, ensuring consistency and continuity by involving the same GDG members as those who contributed to the original ANC guideline. The updated guideline specifically addresses antenatal vitamin D supplementation. It concludes that oral vitamin D supplementation is not recommended for all pregnant women to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes. This recommendation does not alter the corresponding guidance previously issued in the 2016 ANC guideline. Pregnant women should instead be encouraged to achieve adequate nutrition through a healthy, balanced diet and to refer to guidelines on healthy eating. Additionally, sunlight exposure remains the most important source of vitamin D, though the required duration of sun exposure varies based on factors such as skin pigmentation, time of day, latitude, season, and sunscreen use. For pregnant women suspected of having vitamin D deficiency, supplementation may be provided at the current recommended nutrient intake of 200 IU (5 µg) per day. This may include women in populations with limited direct sun exposure. The target audience for this updated recommendation includes national and local public health policymakers, maternal and child health program implementers and managers, professional bodies, healthcare professionals, and academic staff involved in health professional training. The guideline development process adhered to WHO’s standardized operating procedures, which include identifying priority questions, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, assessing the evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, and evaluation. The scientific evidence supporting the recommendations was synthesized using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach for quantitative evidence and the GRADE-CERQual approach for qualitative evidence. Systematic reviews were used to prepare evidence profiles for the prioritized recommendations. The DECIDE framework, an evidence-to-decision tool, guided the formulation and approval of the recommendations by the GDG. The WHO technical consultation resulted in a single recommendation regarding antenatal vitamin D supplementation. The GDG had the option to recommend, not recommend, or conditionally recommend the intervention based on specific contexts, targeted monitoring, and evaluation, or in the context of rigorous research. Additional remarks provided by the GDG should be referred to for further information on the basis of this recommendation.
